strengths: The paper is well written, with a good structure and presents the mathematics in a clear and coherent way to the reader.

The proposed minimization of a surrogate function (Sections 3 & 4) is well reinforced with the experiments section, and the motivations in Section 5 are pertinent for such methods to be deployed at scale in the future.
The paper provides a good summary on the existing works of DFL for combinatorial optimization.
The paper propose to combine the methods of smoothing the cost and using a surrogate loss and apply DYS-Net to solve the scalability issue.
Numerical results on common DFL benchmarks are given.

The paper highlights two popular decision-focused learning approaches, smoothing and surrogate losses, and points out reasonable drawbacks of learning with both approaches. It then shows how combining the two approaches may potentially help address weaknesses found in the two approaches. They also show how recently proposed approaches for making DFL more scalable can be combined with surrogate losses to improve scalability and the quality of the learned decisions. They then justify their claims with numerical experiments of a popular set of benchmarks found in PyEPO which highlights some robustness.
Novelty: This paper first introduces a combination of smoothing techniques and a surrogate loss function within the predict-then-optimize framework for combinatorial optimization.

Efficiency: Solving the optimization problem is often the computational bottleneck in PtO. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using DYS-Net, a differentiable solver significantly reducing training time without compromising decision quality.
Clarity: The paper is well-organized and provides clear and thorough explanations. Additionally, visualizations and examples clarify the results and effectively support the theoretical insights.
The ideas are simple and can be easily implemented by practitioners.
You present a good outline of past work and background on existing methods.
The experimental results are promising as well and show improvements of your proposed method against some of the main existing literature.
weaknesses: I am reluctant to accept on contribution grounds.
The majority of the paper is pulling together prior works, with limited novel contribution.

A large portion of the paper is compiling prior problems / works, the surrogate losses in 3.2.1 and 3.2.2 are from existing works, and the experiments (whilst nice and supporting the argument), are toy-experiments and with little differing the cited literature.
Further contribution could be added either via further experimentation or novel theory / mathematics for surrogates (or novel surrogates).

The paper argues that the derivative remains nearly zero for a lot of combinatorial problems but this argument is not verified. It would be better if the authors can give some illustrations based on some examples.
The combination looks straightforward; it is unclear what technical challenges exist to combine the two methods.
It is unclear about the novelty of applying DYS-Net here; it may be just an application.
The empirical results would be more convincing if more ablation empirical studies are given.
The theoretical justification issues stem from the main argument of the paper... however, the surrogate losses ... are inherently convex, so it is unclear why smoothing would be beneficial.
On page 5 there is a proof, but no formal statement. Adding a formal statement that is proved as a lemma or proposition would improve the presentation and precision of the section.

More extensive numerical experiments could be performed, including experiments from recent work that show new smoothing approaches outperform surrogates, to further highlight benefits or drawbacks of combining smoothing with surrogate losses.

The numerical experiments could be expanded to include other methods such as the proposed surrogate loss in [1] and other approaches such as combining regularizers with the surrogate losses and the QP smoothed task loss.
The work still feels somewhat incremental; the contribution is centered around the SCE surrogate loss with a combination of smoothing and DYS-Net, which feels like small upgrades and not novel.
The smoothed SCE loss with DYS-Net is faster as expected but performs comparably with other methods and is not uniformly or clearly the best in any setting; SPO+ and CaVE do similar or better.

It is hard to claim that SCE loss is more attractive as Proposition 1 only holds when the original problem Regret and SCE loss are zero; the authors fail to show that the SCE loss bounds the expected regret.
Lack of theoretical supports: the paper lacks a theory supporting the effectiveness of the QP-based relaxation for ILP.
Lack of comparison with related speed-up techniques; the paper does not compare its approach with other established methods that also aim to accelerate PtO processes.
Insufficient scalability demonstration: experiments are conducted on relatively small instances (e.g., 11-node TSP), limiting understanding of scalability for larger combinatorial problems.
Missing hyperparameter details: the paper does not provide explicit details on specific hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, optimizer configurations, or the smoothing parameter μ.

The exposition and contribution is not very clearly expressed; it is difficult to find where the proposed method is written, the empirical problem is never introduced, and model predictions are not explained well.
The statement about smoothing addressing non-differentiability is not well-supported; the illustration in Figure 1b does not give adequate support and does not generalize.

The subsection 'A deep dive into the gradient landscape' does not adequately explain the behavior of the approach; more theoretical analysis or computational results on gradient behavior in higher dimensions are needed.
Section 5 seems misplaced; it explains methods used in a different paper rather than contributing to this work and would be better placed in the appendix.
For the experiments, more details are needed: problem sizes, exact mathematical formulations, architecture details, hyperparameters, and data generation process and dataset statistics.
